\section*{Score-I papers}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI06-P1-PHY-S1-Q03, source={Score-I - Test 06 (28 Jan 2022)}, paper=1, qno=3, type=single, subtopic={Vernier and screw gauge}, answer={B}, answer_src=key, difficulty=3, diff_parts={K1 S1 I1 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: reading of vernier calipers with 8 divisions coinciding with 7 main divisions | steps: least count = 1 mm/8; main scale reading plus coincidence times least count}]
The main scale of vernier callipers reads in millimetre and its vernier is divided into 8 divisions, which coincide with 5 divisions of main scale. When two jaws of instrument touch each other the zero of the vernier coincide with the zero of main scale. A rod is tightly placed along its length between both jaws, it is observed that the zero vernier scale lies just left to 36$^\text{th}$ division of main scale and fourth division of vernier scale coincide with the main scale. Then the measured value is --
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{3.66 cm}
\opt{B}{3.55 cm}
\opt{C}{3.65 cm}
\opt{D}{3.56 cm}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI06-P1-PHY-S1-Q04, source={Score-I - Test 06 (28 Jan 2022)}, paper=1, qno=4, type=single, subtopic={Errors and measurement}, answer={C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=3, diff_parts={K1 S1 I1 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: calculation reported with correct significant figures | steps: apply rules for addition and multiplication; round to least precise}]

\[\dfrac{10{,}569-958.82-1.8\times10^{-1}}{0.9950+8.60+0.015}\]
\begin{qoptions}

\opt{B}{$1\times10^3$}
\opt{C}{$1.00\times10^3$}
\opt{D}{All of these}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI06-P1-PHY-S2-Q12, source={Score-I - Test 06 (28 Jan 2022)}, paper=1, qno=12, type=multi, subtopic={Errors and measurement}, answer={B}, answer_src=key, difficulty=5, diff_parts={K1 S2 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: power values in an AC or DC circuit | steps: power dissipated in each resistor from the circuit analysis; total power from the source; compare options}]
The universal gravitational constant is measured experimentally using Cavendish's experiment. This experiment is a very precise experiment which gives the value of G as $(6.6742\pm0.0010)\times10^{-11}$ N.m$^2$/kg$^2$. Since the universal gravitational constant has some error in it, using it if we find escape speed and acceleration due to gravity on Earth's surface, our values will have error in it. (Assume mass of Earth = $6.0000\times10^{24}$ kg \& radius of Earth = $6.4000\times10^6$ m.) What will be the maximum percentage error in calculating the escape speed on Earth ? (The measurement of mass of Earth has an error of 0.01 \% and radius of Earth has an error of 0.02\% ):-
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{0.045\%}
\opt{B}{0.0225 \%}
\opt{C}{0.015 \%}
\opt{D}{0.0025\%}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI06-P1-PHY-S3-Q01, source={Score-I - Test 06 (28 Jan 2022)}, paper=1, qno=1, type=numerical, subtopic={Vernier and screw gauge}, answer={9.64}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K2 S2 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: actual reading, a screw gauge with zero error | steps: least count 1/50 mm; zero error correction; reading = main + circular times LC minus error}]
The pitch of screw gauge is 1 mm and its circular scale is divided into 50 divisions. When nothing is put between the studs 44$^\text{th}$ division of circular scale coincides with the reference line and circular scale lies between 3$^\text{rd}$ and 4$^\text{th}$ division of main scale. When a glass plate is placed between the studs, the circular scale lies between 13$^\text{th}$ and 14$^\text{th}$ division of main scale and circular scale reads 26 divisions. Find the thickness of the plate (in mm).
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=SI08-P2-PHY-S1-Q02, source={Score-I - Test 08 (09 Feb 2022)}, paper=2, qno=2, type=multi, subtopic={Experiments}, answer={A,B,C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=7, diff_parts={K2 S3 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: focal length, concave lens by optical bench with auxiliary convex lens | steps: convex lens forms image; concave lens placed; displacement method; focal length; errors; check}]
Ram performs optical bench experiment to find out the focal length of a concave lens. For this purpose, he first takes a convex lens and measures the position of object needle and image needle. Then he combines convex lens and concave lens and again measures the object needle and image needle position. The optical bench has no bench error. The readings obtained by Ram in the two experiments are shown in the table below.
\begin{center}\small\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}
\begin{tabular}{|p{1.9cm}|c|c|c|}\hline
 & Object needle & Lens & Image needle\\ \hline
Convex lens & 37.1 cm & 50.6 cm & 77.6 cm\\ \hline
Convex and Concave lens & 37.1 cm & 50.6 cm & 91.1 cm\\ \hline
\end{tabular}\end{center}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{The focal length of the convex lens is 9.0 cm.}
\opt{B}{The focal length of the concave lens is 81 cm in modulus.}
\opt{C}{The error in focal length of convex lens is approximately 0.1 cm.}
\opt{D}{The error in focal length of concave lens is approximately 1.0 cm.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

The smallest division on the main scale of a Vernier calipers is 0.1 cm. Ten divisions of the Vernier scale correspond to nine divisions of the main scale. The figure below on the left shows the reading of this calipers with no gap between its two jaws. The figure on the right shows the reading with a solid sphere held between the jaws. The correct diameter of the sphere is
\bfig{206.5}{SI09_p1_phy_s1_q01_1.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{3.07 cm}
\opt{B}{3.11 cm}
\opt{C}{3.15 cm}
\opt{D}{3.17 cm}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI09-P2-PHY-S1-Q04, source={Score-I - Test 09 (16 Feb 2022)}, paper=2, qno=4, type=multi, subtopic={Units and dimensions}, answer={B,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K2 S2 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: dimensions of the Poynting-like quantity S, others | steps: S = (E x B)/mu0 has dimension of energy per area per time; compare with listed quantities; check}]
A physical quantity $\vec S$ is defined as $\vec S=(\vec E\times\vec B)/\mu_0$, where $\vec E$ is electric field, $\vec B$ is magnetic field and $\mu_0$ is the permeability of free space. The dimensions of $\vec S$ are the same as the dimensions of which of the following quantity(ies) ?
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$\dfrac{\text{Energy}}{\text{charge}\times\text{current}}$}
\opt{B}{$\dfrac{\text{Force}}{\text{Length}\times\text{Time}}$}
\opt{C}{$\dfrac{\text{Energy}}{\text{Volume}}$}
\opt{D}{$\dfrac{\text{Power}}{\text{Area}}$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI10-P1-PHY-S1-Q07, source={Score-I - Test 10 (24 Feb 2022)}, paper=1, qno=7, type=multi, subtopic={Errors and measurement}, answer={A,C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=2, diff_parts={K1 S1 I0 C0 F1}, diff_note={concepts: least-count error and propagation in a pendulum | steps: period error is least count over 20 oscillations = 0.05 s; percentage error in g is twice the percentage error in T = 5 percent}]
A student uses a simple pendulum of exactly 1 m length to determine $g$, the acceleration due to gravity. He uses a stop watch with the least count of 1 sec for this and records 40 seconds for 20 oscillations. For this observation, which of the following statement(s) is (are) true?
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{Error $\Delta T$ in measuring $T$, the time period is 0.05 seconds}
\opt{B}{Error $\Delta T$ in measuring $T$, the time period is 1 second}
\opt{C}{Percentage error in the determination of $g$ is 5\%}
\opt{D}{Percentage error in the determination of $g$ is 2.5\%}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI11-P1-PHY-S2-Q09, source={Score-I - Test 11 (27 Feb 2022)}, paper=1, qno=9, type=multi, subtopic={Units and dimensions}, answer={A,B}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K1 S3 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: relations among exponents when all quantities are expressed through one quantity X | steps: speed = position over time so time exponent alpha - beta; acceleration p = beta - (alpha - beta); momentum and force exponents through mass; solve relations; check options}, also_in={JEE Advanced (2021 Series) - Test 02 (04 Feb 2021) P1 Q9}]
Sometimes it is convenient to construct a system of units so that all quantities can be expressed in terms of only one physical quantity. In one such system, dimensions of different quantities are given in terms of a quantity $X$ as follows: [position] $=[X^{\alpha}]$; [speed] $=[X^{\beta}]$; [acceleration] $=[X^{p}]$; [linear momentum] $=[X^{q}]$; [force] $=[X^{r}]$. Then -
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$\alpha+p=2\beta$}
\opt{B}{$p+q-r=\beta$}
\opt{C}{$p-q+r=\alpha$}
\opt{D}{$p+q+r=\beta$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI11-P2-PHY-S2-Q03, source={Score-I - Test 11 (27 Feb 2022)}, paper=2, qno=3, type=numerical, subtopic={Errors and measurement}, answer={1.30}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K2 S2 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: percentage error, energy stored in two capacitors in series | steps: C_eq = C1 C2/(C1 + C2); relative error through partial derivatives; energy = (1/2) C V^2 so error = error C + 2 error V; evaluate}]

\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=SI24-P1-PHY-S1-Q02, source={Score-I - Test 24 (11 Dec 2022)}, paper=1, qno=2, type=single, subtopic={Errors and measurement}, answer={D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=4, diff_parts={K1 S3 I1 C0 F0}, diff_note={concepts: statements on significant figures | steps: count significant figures in 0.31 times 10^3; perimeter rounding to decimal places of the least precise; division keeps least number of significant figures; subtraction keeps decimal places; check each}]
Choose correct statement(s) :

(1) The number of significant figures in $0.31\times10^{3}$ m is two.

(2) The length and breadth of a rectangular sheet are 4.234 m and 1.00 m then the perimeter of rectangle with correct number of significant figures is 10.46 m.

(3) When 97.52 m is divided by 2.54 s, the result with correct number of significant figures is 38.393.

(4) When 0.2 J is subtracted from 7.26 J, then result with correct number of significant figure is 7.1 J.
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{Only 1 and 2 are correct.}
\opt{B}{Only 1, 2 and 3 are correct.}
\opt{C}{Only 2 and 3 are correct.}
\opt{D}{Only 1 and 4 are correct.}
\end{qoptions}

\begin{bankq}[id=SI24-P1-PHY-S3-Q08, source={Score-I - Test 24 (11 Dec 2022)}, paper=1, qno=8, type=numerical, subtopic={Errors and measurement}, answer={4}, answer_src=key, difficulty=7, diff_parts={K2 S2 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: maximum percentage error in frequency from length, radius of an open pipe | steps: f = v/(2 (l + 1.2 r)) for fundamental with end correction; relative error of the combined length term from errors in l and r; evaluate maximum percentage; multiply by 25 | I: end correction couples radius and length errors}]
A open organ pipe containing air resonates in fundamental mode due to a tuning fork. The measurement value of length $\ell$ (in cm) of the pipe are $\ell=94.0\pm0.1$, $r=5.0\pm0.05$. The velocity of the sound in air is accurately known. The maximum percentage error in the measurement of the frequency of that tuning fork by thus experiment, will be $\alpha$, then find the value of $25\alpha$.
\end{bankq}

\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{The standard of length in each of these two systems are related to each other as $\ell'=\frac{\alpha^3}{\beta^3}\ell$.}
\opt{B}{The standard of mass in each of these two systems are related to each other as $m'=\left(\frac{1}{\alpha^2\beta^2}\right)m$.}
\opt{C}{The standard of time in each of these two systems are related to each other as $t'=\left(\frac{\alpha}{\beta^2}\right)t$.}
\opt{D}{The standard of momentum in each of these two systems are related to each other as $p'=\left(\frac{1}{\beta^3}\right)p$.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=PS02-P1-PHY-S1-Q03, source={Pre-Score (2023-24) - Test 02 (15 Oct 2023)}, paper=1, qno=3, type=multi, subtopic={Errors and measurement}, answer={B}, answer_src=key, working={Printed key.}, difficulty=5, diff_parts={K1 S2 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: percentage and absolute errors in heights | steps: difference in height at two ages; errors add in a difference; fractional error of each measurement; compare relative errors | I: error in a difference adds absolutely | C: arithmetic with several measured values}]
Twins Anna and Tom measure each other's heights each birthday. When they were 12 Anna's height was measured as 151.5 cm and Tom's was measured as 151 cm. On their 16th birthday Anna's height is measured as 167.5 cm and Tom's is measured as 168.5 cm. The uncertainty in the height measurements is 5 mm. Anna and Tom have always been very competitive about their heights, so Tom crows with glee after being measured, saying ``Finally, I'm taller than you! We were always about the same height, but now I'm taller than you!'' Anna responds, ``You're crazy! I was clearly taller than you when we were 12.'' Which of the following statements is most correct?
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{Tom is probably right and Anna is wrong, they were about the same height at 12, with a difference of 0.5 cm $\pm$ 1.0 cm. Now the measurements show the difference to be 1.0 cm $\pm$ 1.0 cm, more accurate measurements would resolve the dispute over who is taller now.}
\opt{B}{Tom is probably right and Anna is wrong, they were about the same height at 12, with a difference of 0.5 cm $\pm$ 1.0 cm. Now the measurements show the difference to be 1.0 cm $\pm$ 1.0 cm, however, taking more measurements, regardless of how accurate, couldn't help resolve the dispute over who is taller now.}
\opt{C}{Anna is right and Tom is wrong, Anna was taller at 12, with a difference of 0.5 cm $\pm$ 0.5 cm. Now Tom is taller by 1.0 cm $\pm$ 0.5 cm.}
\opt{D}{Anna is right and Tom is wrong, she was 0.5 cm taller than Tom when they were 12. Tom is now 1.0 cm taller than Anna.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankpassage}[id=PS02-P1-PHY-S2-G7-8, source={Pre-Score (2023-24) - Test 02 (15 Oct 2023)}, questions={7-8}]
The spherometer is used to measure thickness of thin plates and radius of curvature of spherical surfaces. The principle of measurement in the spherometer is same as that of the screw gauge. The circular scale of the spherometer is rotated by a right-handed screw. When the circular scale rotates in the counter-clockwise direction it moves up. Before making any measurement, the three legs of the circular scale are placed on a plane level surface and the screw is rotated so that its tip touches the surface. In this position, if the zero mark of the main scale does not coincide with the zero mark of the circular scale, the instrument is said to possess a zero error. If the zero mark of the circular scale lies a little ahead (in the direction of rotation) of that of the main scale, the zero error is taken to be positive. If the zero mark of the circular scale lies a little behind that of the main scale, the zero error is negative. In the spherometer shown in fig(a), the total number of divisions on the circular scale of the spherometer is 200 and 5 divisions of the main scale is equal to 10 mm. When the spherometer is given one rotation it travels a distance of one division on the main scale. This is called the pitch of the spherometer. In the level position of the legs and the screw, the zero mark of the circular scale lies 50 divisions (of the circular scale) behind the zero mark of the main scale. When thickness of the plate is measured, 45$^{\mathrm{th}}$ division of the circular scale lies in between 2$^{\mathrm{nd}}$ and 3$^{\mathrm{rd}}$ division of the main scale.
\end{bankpassage}
